newsitem.title: USA: Rubin visits Vietnam, wears funny hat, moves on.
newsitem.headline: Rubin visits Vietnam, wears funny hat, moves on.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin was the highest-ranking U.S. economic official to visit Hanoi since the Vietnam War ended in 1975, so the recently reopened American embassy there was leaving nothing to chance.

Even before Rubin arrived, embassy officials were warning that Hanoi might try to embarass him by forcing him to ride around in the black Cadillac used by Graham Martin, America's last ambassador to its former war-time ally, South Vietnam.

In the event, that did not happen, although Treasury officials had an anxious moment when a black car rolled up to meet the secretary's plane after its arrived last Sunday from the Philippines during his just-concluded Asian trip.
A quick check determined it was not the notorious Cadillac reviled as a wartime symbol by the former North Vietnamese.
Speaking to reporters en route home early Wednesday after a six-day trip including two in Vietnam, Rubin said he did not feel the war's legacy would block improved ties.
"The sense I had was the opposite," he said. "They're anxious to have full relations with the United States."

Rubin may no longer be the political novice he was when he first joined the Clinton administration over four years ago, but that did not stop him from breaking in Hanoi one of his own rules for success in the hurly-burly of Washington.

Rubin, who found himself forced to wear an oversized, wide-brimmed straw hat when he visited an 11th century temple in Hanoi this week, later ruefully admitted to businessmen that he had allowed himself to be photographed with it on.

"You remember Dukakis in the tank with a hat on?" he asked on Monday, referring to ex-Massachusetts Gov. Michael Dukakis, who was photographed peering from a tank turret in an outsized helmet during his losing 1988 presidential campaign.
"One of the things that I've learned in this business is not to let yourself get photographed wearing a hat," he added.
But that that fate befell him at the Temple of Literature and National University as Rubin was presented with what he later called "a funny little hat" given to graduates.
He could hardly refuse. The photographers -- not to mention the television cameraman -- loved it. Rubin did not.
"You could watch the centuries peel away," Rubin said Monday of his half-hour drive to Bat Trang, a village just outside Hanoi, along a dirt road atop an ancient dike.
The motorcade of officials and reporters swept by rice paddies, brick kilns, bemused farmers and countless water buffalo before arriving in the so-called ceramic village.

A road in the village was so narrow that Treasury officials at first could barely open the doors of their cars to get out because they were surrounded by men and women selling vegetables, fruits and spices.
Charcoal patties, formed by the villagers and imprinted with handprints, were slapped on the sides of many of the buildings to dry before being used for heat.

After a frantic few minutes snapping up souvenirs -- Rubin just watched in amusement -- Treasury officials jumped back into their cars and roared off to catch a plane to Ho Chi Minh City for further meetings on mending ties with Vietnam.
For many of the U.S. Secret Service detail accompanying Rubin to Vietnam, the return to Ho Chi Minh City -- the former Saigon -- was a homecoming of sorts.

At least four of the agents guarding Rubin during his two-day Vietnam sojourn had served in the military during the Vietnam War. One had earned the Congressional Medal of Honour for his exploits with U.S. Army Special Forces there.

Another ran into a former North Vietnamese soldier now with Vietnam's Finance Ministry who served in the same area at the same time as the American did during the war. The two men joked that they had probably been shooting at each other and were now glad they had missed.
The Secret Service is under the jurisdiction of Treasury. Its officials prefer to remain anonymous.
